subject: Accounting
title: The Laffer Curve
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Laffer Curve.

hook.text: Economist Arthur Laffer drew a curve on a napkin that changed tax policy forever.

buildup.text: The idea: at 0% tax, revenue is zero. At 100% tax, no one works—so revenue is also zero.

discovery.text: Somewhere in between is an optimal rate that maximizes revenue. That's the Laffer Curve.

twist.text: Politicians love citing it to justify tax cuts, but no one agrees on where the peak actually is.

climax.text: The curve is more concept than formula—useful for debate but nearly impossible to pinpoint.

punchline.text: The curve is famous. The optimal rate is still unknown.

quiz.question: What does the Laffer Curve illustrate?
options: There's an optimal tax rate that maximizes revenue
Tax cuts always pay for themselves

details.summary: The Laffer Curve illustrates that there's an optimal tax rate for maximizing government revenue — too low and revenue is insufficient, too high and people reduce work or evade taxes, decreasing total collections.
details.whyItMatters: The Laffer Curve is one of the most influential (and debated) concepts in tax policy, used to justify both tax cuts and tax increases depending on where a country sits on the curve.
takeaways: At a 0% tax rate, government collects nothing; at 100%, nobody works and revenue is also zero
Somewhere between these extremes is a rate that maximizes revenue, but economists debate where it is
The Laffer Curve was influential in the 1980s Reagan tax cuts and remains central to tax policy debates

faq.question: What is the Laffer Curve?
faq.answer: It's an economic concept showing that government tax revenue first increases as tax rates rise from zero, but eventually decreases as rates get too high because people work less, invest less, or evade taxes. The peak of the curve represents the revenue-maximizing rate.

faq.question: Is the Laffer Curve accurate?
faq.answer: The basic concept is logical and accepted by economists — at the extremes of 0% and 100%, revenue is indeed zero. The debate is where the peak is. Most evidence suggests developed countries are usually on the left side of the curve, meaning rate cuts reduce rather than increase revenue.
